findings.title: No visual identity: the harbour's world appears only in the copy, on a category-default frame
findings.description: Across all five routes the identity-carrying elements are a stock anchor glyph beside the name set in the body sans, a dark petrol-blue button and a pale blue-grey ground. All three specificity tests fail on this layer (swap with a campsite or library booking; category-guess predicts anchor + navy; a canal-permit brief lands on the same frame). The product's differentiator, arriving only around high water over the sill, is told in words but never shown.
findings.impact: Skippers new to the harbour may not form any memory of Saltmarsh Quay as a place, and the page gives no visual cue that tide timing is the thing to get right; the design does not help the brief's central idea land.

evidence.detail: header anchor + name, native form, petrol button
DESIGN.md missing: no attributes, colour strategy or signature recorded

findings.recommendation: Write the missing DESIGN.md first: decide attributes from the harbour's own world (its tide, sill gate, pontoons and mud berths) and choose a signature drawn from that mechanism, then let type, colour and the name-as-mark carry it on every surface while keeping the forms conventional.

findings.title: Browser-default date input and selects left unthemed on the first screen
findings.description: The arrival date shows the browser's 'yyyy/mm/dd' placeholder and system calendar glyph, and 'Nights' and 'Arrival time' show native select chevrons, the only controls in the product left at their defaults.
findings.impact: The first thing every skipper touches looks unfinished, and the 'yyyy/mm/dd' order clashes with the en-GB 'Saturday 17 October 2026' format used everywhere else, which may cause hesitation entering the date.
findings.recommendation: Decide how the date and time controls present themselves in the product's own type and border system and in en-GB order, keeping native behaviour where it serves phones.

findings.title: Footer band ends mid-viewport on short pages, leaving a grey band beneath
findings.description: On /boat.html, /review.html, /confirmed.html and the 'Booking stopped' state at 1280, the white footer band stops partway down the viewport and the pale grey page ground continues below it.
findings.impact: The page looks cut off or still loading, which undermines confidence at the confirmation step in particular.
findings.recommendation: Decide whether the footer sits at the viewport bottom on short pages or the ground below it matches the footer.

findings.title: Overflow '...' button stranded at the far right of the berth step, hiding 'Change dates'
findings.description: On /berths.html the only route to 'Change dates' is a bordered '...' button placed at the right edge of the container (about x 1028-1072 at 1280), far from the 752px card column, with an empty band between the summary line and the list. The menu opens as a small popover.
findings.impact: Changing the arrival date is a core task, and an unlabelled glyph detached from the dates it changes may be overlooked; the stray button also pulls the eye away from the berth list.
findings.recommendation: Decide where changing the dates belongs relative to the 'Arriving on…' summary so the action is visible and labelled where the dates are stated.

findings.title: Tide table column headings misaligned with right-aligned times
findings.description: 'Morning' and 'Afternoon' headers are left-aligned while the times below them are right-aligned, so at 1280/1440 'Morning' sits over empty space and the 02:08 column reads as belonging to no header.
findings.impact: The tide table is the data skippers use to pick an arrival time; misaligned headings make it slower to read morning versus afternoon high water at a glance in a cockpit.
findings.recommendation: Align numeric column headers with their figures.

findings.title: Invalid-field styling inconsistent across error states
findings.description: In each error state one invalid field keeps a dark border while its invalid siblings turn red: 'Length' on /boat.html errors, 'Skipper's name' on /review.html errors, 'Arrival time' on / errors. Stills cannot show whether this is a focus style overriding the error border.
findings.impact: Skippers scanning for what to fix may read the dark-bordered field as valid; the error system looks unreliable.
findings.recommendation: Decide how error and focus states combine so an invalid field always shows its error treatment.

findings.title: The tide window, the product's differentiator, is disconnected from the arrival-time choice
findings.description: The intro says to plan around high water, but the 'Arrival time' select gives no gate-window cue; the tide table sits below the button (fully below the fold at 375) and states times in UTC, while arrival times elsewhere are shown as local ('at 15:00'). The berth and confirmation steps do not mention the gate window for the chosen day.
findings.impact: Skippers may pick an arrival time outside the sill-gate window, or misread the window by an hour in British Summer Time; the one thing that makes this harbour different is presented as a side table instead of shaping the choice.

evidence.detail: tide table begins at y≈730, after 'Check berths'
'High water at the quay, times in UTC' vs 'Arriving on Saturday 17 October 2026 at 15:00'
no gate window or arrival time on confirmation

findings.recommendation: Decide how the gate window for the chosen date informs the arrival-time choice, and use one time basis throughout; this is also the natural candidate for the product's signature.

findings.title: 'Booking stopped' state is a bare dead end
findings.description: When the boat is over the berth's length limit, the page replaces the form with 'Booking stopped' and 'This booking cannot continue. Reference BK-409.' with no reason, no link back to choose another berth, and the footer floating at y≈222 at 1280.
findings.impact: A skipper whose boat is too long for the chosen pontoon (the wall berth takes up to 15 m) may abandon the booking and phone the office instead.
findings.recommendation: Decide what this state should say and offer (the reason and a route to a berth that fits) and design it as a state, not an empty page.

findings.title: Content hugs the left of the container at wide widths, leaving the right half empty
findings.description: At 1280 and 1440 every route places a 320px form column (cards 544px) in the left part of a ~864px container while the header nav sits at the far right, so the right half of each page is empty ground.
findings.impact: Wide views on the desktop look half-built; the evening-before planning on a laptop meets an emptier page than the phone view.
findings.recommendation: Decide what the wide layout is for (for example, keeping the tide information beside the arrival choice) or narrow the container so the column and header align.

findings.title: One-word last lines in headings and summary values at 320/375
findings.description: H1 'Choose a pontoon space' breaks to leave 'space' alone at 375 and 320; review H1 leaves 'booking'; the review summary leaves '15:00' and 'arrival' on their own lines at 320.
findings.impact: Minor polish at phone widths, the primary context; stranded words make headings look unconsidered.
findings.recommendation: Balance heading wraps at narrow widths.

_strengths: Berth cards carry real, useful harbour content: length limit, tidal behaviour ('Afloat at every state of the tide' / 'Settles on soft mud at low water') and price per metre per night.

The flow is calm and conventional for an Operate journey: one primary action per step, labels above fields, specific error messages with an error summary, and a clear key/value check page with the payment reassurance 'Nothing is charged online.'
Clean, legible light palette with strong text contrast suits bright-light phone use.
_keep: Keep the plain-spoken, harbour-specific copy and the one-action-per-step structure; add identity around them, not inside the forms.
